title: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
summary: Why search runs cheap high-recall stages before costly rerankers: recall ceilings, per-stage latency budgets, a learned GBDT middle stage, LLM reranking, distillation, and a measured SciFact cascade.
outcomes: Explain why a reranker can never exceed the recall of the candidate list it receives, and choose candidate depth k or a score cutoff
Compute the latency of a 3-stage cascade from per-stage depth, throughput and sequence length and fit it to a budget
Compare bi-encoders, ColBERT late interaction and cross-encoders by when query and document meet, and compute MaxSim
Place a LambdaMART middle stage over first-stage features and use reranker scores as features instead of overwriting the order
Trace a sliding-window listwise LLM reranker and count its calls
Compute Margin-MSE, KL and RankNet distillation losses and explain what each pushes the student to fix
Measure a cascade stage by stage: recall@k curves, rerank depth sweeps against an oracle, paired tests and time per stage

lessons.title: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate

blocks.md:
The most accurate relevance models read the query and a document **together**. A cross-encoder such as monoBERT (Nogueira and Cho, 2019) feeds `[CLS] query [SEP] passage` through BERT, the pretrained transformer from Google (2018). `[CLS]` is a special token placed first, and `[SEP]` is the separator token that marks where the query ends and the passage begins. BERT's output vector at the `[CLS]` position goes through one small neural layer that outputs a probability of relevance. Nothing can be precomputed, because every score depends on both texts.

Khattab and Zaharia measured what that costs. BERT-base is the 12-layer, 110-million-parameter version of BERT (BERT-large has 24 layers and 340 million). BERT-base reranking BM25's top 1000 MS MARCO passages took 10,700 ms per query on one Tesla V100 GPU. That is about 10.7 ms per passage.

blocks.prompt: MS MARCO has 8.8 million passages. At 10.7 ms per passage, how long would BERT-base need to score the whole collection for a single query?
blocks.reveal: 8.8 million x 10.7 ms = 94,160 seconds, about **26 hours per query**. Even a 100x faster GPU would leave you at roughly 16 minutes. Exhaustive scoring with the best model is not an engineering problem you can tune away; you need to score far fewer documents.

blocks.md: The way out is a **cascade** (also called multi-stage ranking or retrieve-then-rerank). Wang, Lin and Metzler (SIGIR 2011) describe it as a sequence of increasingly complex ranking functions that progressively prune documents and refine the order of the survivors. Early stages are cheap and see many documents; later stages are expensive and see few. They borrowed the intuition from Viola and Jones' face detector, which rejects easy negatives with simple classifiers before running costly ones.

blocks.caption: Wang, Lin and Metzler's cost model: stage t costs its per-document unit cost U_t times the number of documents R_t it scores; summing over all T stages gives the query's total cost C(q). Each stage passes a shorter list k_t to the next one.

blocks.title: A three-stage cascade: BM25, then monoBERT, then duoBERT

scenes.caption: Nogueira, Yang, Cho and Lin (2019) build this pipeline on MS MARCO and number its stages H0, H1 and H2. The corpus holds 8.8M passages; the query cannot afford a neural model on all of them.

Stage H0: BM25 over an inverted index returns k0 = 1000 candidates (Anserini, an open-source toolkit built on Lucene: about 62 ms per query). Its job is recall: get the relevant passages somewhere into the list.
Stage H1: monoBERT scores each of the 1000 candidates independently (1000 inferences) and keeps the top k1 = 50.
Stage H2: duoBERT compares ordered pairs of the 50 survivors: 50 x 49 = 2450 inferences, more than monoBERT's 1000, but only on a list it could afford.
The final list goes to the user (or, in retrieval-augmented generation, into an LLM's prompt so it answers from those passages). Every stage only reorders and truncates what it was given.

blocks.md: **monoBERT** is *pointwise*: it scores one (query, passage) pair at a time. **duoBERT** is *pairwise*: given (query, $d_i$, $d_j$) it estimates $p_{ij}$, the probability that $d_i$ is more relevant than $d_j$. Those pair scores are folded back into one score per passage, for example by summing:

blocks.caption: duoBERT's SUM aggregation. The paper also tested BINARY (count wins with p above 0.5), MIN and MAX (use only the smallest or largest p_ij, i.e. the strongest or weakest rival) and SAMPLE (sum over a random subset); MAX made results worse than monoBERT alone.

blocks.md:
Quality here is **MRR@10**: for each query, take the reciprocal rank, 1 over the rank of the first relevant passage in the top 10 (0 if none is there), then take the mean over queries; a first hit at rank 2 earns 0.5, and papers report the mean times 100. MS MARCO dev is the public set of labeled development queries; the evaluation set's labels are hidden and only the organizers score it.

On MS MARCO dev, MRR@10 went from 18.7 (Anserini BM25) to 37.2 with monoBERT and 38.2 with monoBERT plus duoBERT-SUM; on the held-out evaluation set duoBERT added 0.5 points. The paper's point is not only the final number: because each stage controls how many candidates it admits, you can pick an operating point on the quality versus latency curve.

Each stage has a different job. The first stage must not lose relevant documents (recall); precision barely matters there, because later stages discard junk. The last stage must put the best documents on top (precision at the top) and only has to be good on a short list.
A reranker never finds anything. It can only reorder the list it receives. If stage 1 missed a document, no later stage, however large, can bring it back.

blocks.question: Why does the pipeline run duoBERT on monoBERT's top 50 instead of directly on BM25's top 1000?
options: duoBERT cannot read passages that BM25 retrieved
Pairwise scoring grows as k(k-1): 1000 candidates would need 999,000 inferences instead of 2450
duoBERT is less accurate than monoBERT, so it should see fewer documents
BM25 scores must be normalized before a pairwise model can use them
blocks.explain: Pairwise cost is quadratic in the list length. On 1000 candidates, duoBERT would need 1000 x 999 = 999,000 inferences per query, about 290 times the 3450 that monoBERT plus duoBERT on 50 use. Putting the quadratic model last, on a short list, is exactly the cascade idea.

blocks.question: Under Wang, Lin and Metzler's cost model, you double k0 from 500 to 1000 in a BM25 plus monoBERT pipeline. What happens to monoBERT's cost per query?
options: It stays the same, because monoBERT runs once per query
It grows by about log 2
It roughly doubles, because cost is unit cost times the number of documents scored
It quadruples
blocks.explain: monoBERT scores each candidate independently, so its cost is U x k0. Nogueira et al. report exactly this: latency increases linearly with the number of candidates, while quality shows diminishing returns.

lessons.title: Candidate depth k and the recall ceiling

blocks.md: **Recall@k** is the fraction of a query's relevant documents that appear in the top $k$ of a ranked list. For a cascade, the recall@k of the list that stage 1 hands over (with $k = k_0$) is a hard ceiling on everything after it.

A toy query has **4 relevant documents**. The first stage ranks them at positions 2, 7, 19 and 140. Suppose the reranker is *perfect*: it always puts every relevant candidate it receives on top. How good can the final top 10 be?

blocks.title: Rerank depth k decides what the perfect reranker can see

scenes.caption: The first 20 positions of the stage 1 list. R marks a relevant document; the fourth relevant one sits at rank 140, off screen.
k = 5: only the document at rank 2 is passed on. Recall@5 = 1/4 = 0.25, so even a perfect reranker's top 10 holds 1 of 4 relevant documents.
k = 10: ranks 2 and 7 are in. Recall@10 = 0.5. The reranker can move both to the top, but cannot invent the other two.
k = 20: rank 19 joins. Recall@20 = 0.75, and the best possible final recall@10 is now 0.75.
k = 100 still gives 0.75: nothing new between 20 and 100. Any k of at least 140 reaches the last relevant document and recall 1.0; k = 200, for example, costs 10 times the reranking of k = 20.

blocks.caption: The ceiling. Rel is the set of relevant documents for the query and Top_k is what stage 1 passes on. Any metric that only rewards relevant documents (MRR, nDCG, recall) is capped the same way.

blocks.md:
**nDCG@10** handles graded relevance: each of the top 10 documents adds a gain that grows with its relevance grade, discounted by dividing by the base-2 logarithm of its rank plus 1. That sum is the discounted cumulative gain, and dividing it by the best possible sum normalizes it: normalized discounted cumulative gain, or nDCG, on which a perfect order scores 1.

ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020, the paper whose BERT-base timing we used in lesson 1) is a neural scorer that precomputes vectors for every passage. So it can be used two ways: to rerank a list it is handed, or to search the whole collection itself through a vector index. Lesson 3 shows how it scores.

blocks.prompt: Khattab and Zaharia report two ColBERT setups on MS MARCO dev. One reranks the official BM25 top 1000; the other retrieves end to end with its own vector index. The model is the same. Which has higher MRR@10, and why?
blocks.reveal: End to end wins: **36.0** versus **34.8** MRR@10. Reranking BM25's list caps recall@1000 at 81.4%, the recall of the BM25 list itself. End-to-end ColBERT reaches 96.8% recall@1000, so it can surface relevant passages that BM25 never retrieved. Same scorer, higher ceiling.

blocks.md: One more first stage appears in the next chart. **docTTTTTquery** (Nogueira and Lin, 2019) is document expansion: before indexing, a T5 model (Google's Text-To-Text Transfer Transformer; the five T's give the name) writes questions each passage might answer, and they are appended to the passage. Plain BM25 can then match queries that use words the passage itself lacked.

blocks.title: Recall of different first stages on MS MARCO dev (%)

scenes.caption: Recall@50. A cheap first stage keeps only 59.2% of relevant passages in its top 50 (Anserini BM25). Document expansion (docTTTTTquery) and ColBERT do much better at the same depth.
Recall@200. Going 4x deeper buys BM25 another 14.6 points. End-to-end ColBERT is already at 92.3%.

Recall@1000. ColBERT reranking the official MS MARCO BM25 top 1000 (a weaker run than Anserini's 85.7%) is stuck at 81.4%, exactly that list's recall: the ceiling in action. End-to-end ColBERT reaches 96.8%.

blocks.md:
Deeper is better for recall, but not proportionally for quality. Nogueira et al. varied $k_0$ for monoBERT: compared with $k_0 = 1000$, they got more than half of the quality gain with about a fifth of the inferences. They also note that a deep list makes monoBERT score documents with quite low BM25 scores, which shows how weak BM25's own ordering is lower down.

The right $k$ is where stage 1's recall curve flattens, subject to the latency budget of the next stage (lesson 4).

Measure stage 1 on its own. Log recall@k for k in 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 on a labeled query set. If recall is low, upgrading the reranker is wasted money: improve the first stage (hybrid retrieval, document expansion, a better embedding model) or raise k.

So far every query got the same depth. When the last stage feeds an LLM (retrieval-augmented generation), a fixed top 5 wastes context on easy queries and can starve hard ones. A **score cutoff** keeps every candidate whose reranker score clears a threshold instead, so the number of passages varies per query.

Toy: after reranking, query A's eight candidates have relevance probabilities 0.97, 0.95, 0.20, 0.08, 0.05, 0.03, 0.02, 0.01 and query B's have 0.62, 0.58, 0.55, 0.52, 0.49, 0.47, 0.31, 0.12. A fixed top 5 sends three likely misses for A. A 0.5 cutoff sends 2 passages for A and 4 for B.

blocks.title: Fixed top 5 versus a 0.5 score cutoff (toy probabilities)

scenes.caption: Easy query A: two clear winners, then a cliff. A fixed top 5 also sends ranks 3 to 5 (muted), which the model scores 0.20 and below. The cutoff stops at 2.

Hard query B: no cliff, many borderline scores. The cutoff keeps 4 (ranks 1 to 4); a fixed top 5 keeps one more at 0.49. On hard queries the cutoff and k disagree only slightly; on easy ones they differ a lot.

blocks.md: A cutoff needs scores that mean the same thing across queries, and raw cross-encoder logits do not promise that. In our SciFact test run, when the MS MARCO cross-encoder from *Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval* gave its best candidate (from the RRF top 20) a positive logit, that candidate was relevant for 63% of 235 claims; at or below 0 for 31% of 65. Useful, but far from a calibrated probability. Validate any threshold on labeled queries, and redo it when the model changes.

Wang, Lin and Metzler hit the same problem inside the cascade: "document scores for different queries are different, so enforcing a common score threshold is unlikely to work well." Their pruning functions therefore set the threshold relative to each list: a fraction of the way from the list's minimum to its maximum score, or a mix of its mean and maximum. Later work learns the cut position directly from the scores: Choppy (Bahri et al., 2020) is a small transformer that reads a ranked list's scores and picks the truncation point that optimizes a chosen metric.

blocks.question: Your RAG search uses BM25 top 100 and a strong cross-encoder. You swap in a cross-encoder twice as large and nDCG@10 barely moves. Stage 1 recall@100 is 0.62. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: The new cross-encoder is undertrained
The ceiling: 38% of relevant documents never reach the reranker, so stage 1 recall or k must improve
nDCG@10 cannot measure reranker quality
k = 100 is too deep and confuses the reranker
blocks.explain: With recall@100 of 0.62, the reranker never sees 38% of relevant documents. Bigger rerankers only reorder the 62% they receive. Raise the ceiling: hybrid first stage, better embeddings, or a larger k if the budget allows.

blocks.question: In the toy above (relevant at ranks 2, 7, 19, 140), you rerank the top 20 with a perfect reranker. What is the final recall@10?
blocks.explain: Three relevant documents (ranks 2, 7, 19) are in the top 20; the perfect reranker moves all three into the top 10. The fourth, at rank 140, never arrives. 3/4 = 0.75.

lessons.title: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes

blocks.md:
Every neural scorer in a cascade is defined by **when query and document meet**:

- **Bi-encoder** (dense retrieval): encode query and document separately into one vector each and take a dot product. Document vectors are computed offline and indexed for nearest-neighbor search.
- **Cross-encoder**: concatenate query and document and run the full transformer on the pair. Every layer can compare every query token with every document token, but nothing can be precomputed.
- **Late interaction** (ColBERT): encode each side separately, but keep **one vector per token**, and compare them with a cheap operator at query time.

blocks.title: When do query and document meet?

scenes.caption: Bi-encoder: the document side runs offline. At query time you encode only the query, then one dot product per document, which an ANN index can search over millions of vectors.
Late interaction: still encoded separately (documents offline), but each side keeps a vector per token. The score sums, over query tokens, the best match among document tokens.
Cross-encoder: one transformer reads the pair together, so attention mixes query and document from the first layer. Most accurate, but a full forward pass per (query, document) at query time.

blocks.md: ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, SIGIR 2020) defines the late-interaction score as a sum of maximum similarities. Token vectors are L2-normalized (divided by their Euclidean length, so each has length 1), so each dot product is a cosine in $[-1, 1]$:

blocks.caption: For each query token, find its best-matching document token and add that similarity. Document tokens that match nothing contribute nothing.

blocks.title: MaxSim on toy token embeddings

scenes.caption: Cosines between 3 query tokens and the tokens of doc A (left 5 columns) and doc C (right 5). Vectors are hand-made 5-dimensional toys, not real ColBERT outputs.
Doc A: each query token has a near-perfect partner (reset with reboot 0.99, router 1.00, 651 1.00). MaxSim = 0.99 + 1.00 + 1.00 = 2.99. The off-topic warranty and refund tokens are simply ignored.
Doc C is vaguely about networking. Best matches are only 0.65 (help), 0.84 (modem) and 0.57 (issue): MaxSim = 2.06. Nothing in it mentions error 651.

Mean-pool each side into one vector instead (a crude bi-encoder) and the order flips: cosine 0.864 for C versus 0.711 for A, because A's average is dragged toward its shopping tokens. Per-token matching keeps the precise evidence.

blocks.md: The cost differences are large. Reranking the BM25 top 1000 on MS MARCO with one V100 (Khattab and Zaharia, Table 1):

blocks.title: Reranking BM25 top 1000 on MS MARCO: cost and quality

scenes.caption: Rerank latency per query in ms. ColBERT takes 61 ms, BERT-base 10,700 ms (over 170 times slower) and BERT-large 32,900 ms.
MRR@10 on dev (x 1000 to share the axis): 349, 360 and 365. ColBERT is within about 1 to 1.6 points of the cross-encoders at a tiny fraction of the cost. (Lesson 2's 34.8 is the L2-distance variant.)

blocks.md: Where did ColBERT's 61 ms go? Only 13 ms was query encoding plus interaction; the rest was gathering the precomputed document vectors and moving them to the GPU. Late interaction shifts cost from compute to **storage and memory traffic**: the MS MARCO index with 128-dimensional vectors at 4 bytes per dimension took 286 GiB.

ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022) shrinks this with residual compression. It runs k-means clustering on a sample of token vectors to get a set of **centroids**, typical points in the vector space. Each token vector is stored as the id of its nearest centroid plus the **residual**, the vector minus that centroid, with each of the residual's 128 dimensions quantized to 1 or 2 bits. That is 4 bytes for the id plus 16 or 32 bytes for the residual: 20 or 36 bytes instead of 256 bytes (128 dimensions at 16-bit precision), shrinking the index 6 to 10 times.

Cross-encoders come in other shapes too. **monoT5** (Nogueira, Jiang and Lin, 2020) feeds `Query: q Document: d Relevant:` to T5 (the text-in, text-out model from lesson 2). It is fine-tuned to write the word `true` for a relevant passage and `false` otherwise, so at ranking time it takes the logits of just those two tokens, applies a softmax, and ranks by the probability of `true`. With BM25 top 1000 on MS MARCO dev it scored 0.383 MRR@10 (T5-large) against 0.372 for BERT-large, and it was much more data-efficient with few training examples.

Precompute versus interact. The more of the query-document comparison happens at query time, the more accurate and the more expensive the scorer. Bi-encoders and late interaction can serve as first stages over an index; cross-encoders only fit on short candidate lists.

blocks.question: Which scorer could you put directly over a 50-million-document index as the **first** stage?
options: A cross-encoder, if you batch on a large GPU
A bi-encoder or late-interaction model, because document vectors are precomputed and searchable with ANN
Only BM25; neural models cannot be first stages
duoBERT with the SAMPLE aggregation
blocks.explain: First stages need precomputed document representations so the query can be matched with an index. Bi-encoders give one vector per document; ColBERT indexes token vectors and retrieves end to end. A cross-encoder has nothing to index: it needs a forward pass per pair.

blocks.question: In the MaxSim toy, you append five more unrelated tokens to doc A. What happens to A's MaxSim score?
options: It drops, because the average similarity falls
It rises, because more tokens means more matches
It is unchanged unless a new token beats an existing best match
It becomes undefined because A is longer than the query
blocks.explain: MaxSim takes, for each query token, the maximum over document tokens. Extra tokens can only raise a maximum, never lower it, and unrelated ones (low cosine) leave the maxima at 0.99, 1.00, 1.00. Mean pooling, in contrast, is diluted by them.

lessons.title: Latency budgets and phased ranking in real engines

blocks.md: A cascade is designed backwards from a **latency budget**: the time the product allows for one search, say 150 ms. Using the cost model from lesson 1, each stage costs roughly (candidates scored) x (time per candidate), and the stages run one after another, so their times add up.

We need per-document costs. The Sentence Transformers docs list throughput for their MS MARCO cross-encoders (the Hugging Face model cards say they were measured on a V100 GPU; treat them as relative). MiniLM is Microsoft's small BERT-style transformer, compressed from a larger model; L2, L6 and L12 in the names are its number of layers. TREC DL 19 is the TREC 2019 Deep Learning track: 43 MS MARCO queries whose passages NIST assessors graded on a 0 to 3 scale.

- `ms-marco-MiniLM-L2-v2`: 4100 docs/s, NDCG@10 71.01 on TREC DL 19
- `ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2`: 1800 docs/s, NDCG@10 74.30
- `ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2`: 960 docs/s, NDCG@10 74.31

The 2-layer model is about 4.3 times faster than the 12-layer one and a few points worse: a natural cheap middle stage.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: stage 1 (hybrid retrieval) is assumed to take 20 ms; reranking time is candidates divided by throughput, ignoring batching overheads, network hops and tail effects. Here k_1 and k_2 are the lists entering stages 2 and 3 (lesson 1 called BM25's output k_0).

blocks.title: Accounting for a 3-stage cascade
blocks.code:
def search(query):
    spent = 0.0
    cands = hybrid_retrieve(query, k=200)   # stage 1
    spent += 20.0                           # assumed
    s = minilm_l2.predict([(query, d) for d in cands])
    cands = top(cands, s, k=30)             # stage 2
    spent += 1000 * 200 / 4100
    s = minilm_l12.predict([(query, d) for d in cands])
    final = top(cands, s, k=10)             # stage 3
    spent += 1000 * 30 / 960
    return final, spent

scenes.caption: Stage 1 returns k1 = 200 fused candidates. We assume it costs 20 ms.
Stage 2: the 2-layer cross-encoder scores all 200 at 4100 docs/s: 48.8 ms. It keeps the top 30.
Stage 3: the 12-layer cross-encoder scores only 30 at 960 docs/s: 31.3 ms. The final 10 are returned.
Total about 100 ms, inside a 150 ms budget. Running the 12-layer model on all 200 instead would cost 208.3 ms for that stage alone.

blocks.title: Single expensive stage versus a cascade (simplified model)

scenes.caption: One stage: the 12-layer model on all 200 candidates. 20 + 208.3 = 228.3 ms, far over the 150 ms budget (marker).
Cascade: L2 on 200 (48.8 ms), then L12 on 30 (31.3 ms). Done at 100.0 ms, with 50 ms of headroom.
Spend the headroom on recall: stage 1 passes 400 candidates. L2 now takes 97.6 ms and the total is 148.8 ms, just under budget. Deeper k1 raises the recall ceiling.

blocks.title: Total latency as the middle-stage depth k1 grows

scenes.caption: Defaults: t1 = 20 ms, k2 = 30. The cascade line crosses the 150 ms budget at k1 of about 405; the single 12-layer stage crosses it near k1 = 125.
Raise k2 to 80: the final stage costs 83.3 ms, and the largest affordable k1 falls to about 191. Every stage competes for the same budget.

blocks.md: Documents per second hides a variable: **how many tokens each pair has**. A cross-encoder reads query plus passage, up to its `max_length`. The cost of the linear layers grows in proportion to the tokens, and attention's with their square (*Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together* counts the FLOPs). Batches add a second effect: with `padding=True`, as CrossEncoder uses, Hugging Face tokenizers pad every sequence in a batch to the longest one, so one long passage makes the whole batch pay its length. And a long document split into passages multiplies the pairs: ten chunks are ten forward passes.

blocks.title: ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 throughput by sequence length

scenes.caption: Measured on this machine (CPU, 2 threads, batches of 32, every pair truncated to exactly the length shown, best of 5): about 260, 123 and 53 pairs per second. Doubling 256 to 512 tokens divides throughput by 2.3.

Real SciFact pairs (claim plus title and abstract) have a median of 328 tokens and a 90th percentile of 510: 75% are cut at max_length 256 and 10% even at 512. Choosing max_length is a latency and quality decision at once.

blocks.md: Redo the budget for passages twice as long, assuming both rerankers slow by the same factor 2.3 we measured in one run (a simplification: we have no per-length figures for the V100 numbers). The 2-layer model drops to about 1767 docs/s and the 12-layer one to about 414. The same cascade, 200 then 30, now costs 20 + 113.2 + 72.5 = **205.7 ms**, over the 150 ms budget. To fit, k1 must fall to about 101, so the longer passages cost recall depth. Alternatives: cut max_length, rerank passages instead of whole documents, or buy throughput (on a GPU, larger batches raise pairs per second, but each query waits for its whole batch).

Engines expose the cascade as configuration. **Vespa**, an open-source search engine that began at Yahoo, splits work between *content nodes* (machines that each hold a slice of the documents) and a *stateless container* (the front end that receives the query, fans it out and merges the results). It has explicit phases: a `first-phase` expression runs on every retrieved hit on each content node, a `second-phase` expression reranks the best hits per node (100 by default; `total-rerank-count` caps the total across nodes), and a `global-phase` runs in the stateless container on the merged top hits (100 by default, set with `rerank-count` or the `ranking.globalPhase.rerankCount` query property). The docs name cross-encoders, run as ONNX models (Open Neural Network Exchange, a portable file format for trained models), as the typical global-phase use case.

blocks.title: Phased ranking in Vespa (simplified)

scenes.caption: The stateless container scatters the query to every content node.

Each node retrieves matches (for example with weakAnd, an optimized OR that skips documents unlikely to reach the top hits, or nearest-neighbor operators) and scores all of them with the cheap first-phase expression.
Each node reranks its own best hits with the costlier second-phase expression, close to the data (for example a GBDT model, gradient-boosted decision trees; lesson 5 shows how one is trained).
Nodes return their best hits plus any match-features (feature values computed per hit on the node) the global phase needs.
The container merges, then reranks the global top hits, for example with a cross-encoder in ONNX, possibly on a GPU.

blocks.md: **Elasticsearch** offers two forms. The `rescore` parameter reranks the top `window_size` hits **on each shard** (default 10) with a query, script or learning-to-rank model (one trained to order results from per-document features); several rescorers can run in sequence, and the docs suggest a larger window first and smaller windows for costlier later rescorers. The `text_similarity_reranker` retriever sends the top `rank_window_size` documents (default 10) of a child retriever to a rerank inference endpoint such as a cross-encoder:

blocks.caption: Rerank the top 100 BM25 hits with a cross-encoder endpoint. Without rank_window_size the reranker would only see 10 documents.

blocks.md: Defaults are shallow. Both Elasticsearch's rescore window_size and text_similarity_reranker's rank_window_size default to 10, so an unconfigured reranker can only shuffle the first page. Also keep the window fixed across pages: the docs warn that changing window_size while paginating can make top hits shift.

blocks.question: With t1 = 20 ms, k2 = 30 at 960 docs/s and the cheap reranker at 4100 docs/s, what is the largest k1 that fits a 150 ms budget in this model?
options: About 200
About 1000
About 125
About 400
blocks.explain: The precise stage costs 1000 x 30 / 960 = 31.25 ms. That leaves 150 - 20 - 31.25 = 98.75 ms for the cheap stage, which scores 4.1 docs per ms: 98.75 x 4.1 = 404.9 candidates.

blocks.question: Users report that a relevant document at BM25 rank 15 never moves up, even though the cross-encoder scores it highest when tested alone. The pipeline uses text_similarity_reranker with no extra settings. What is wrong?
options: The cross-encoder needs min_score set to 0
rank_window_size defaults to 10, so the document at rank 15 is never sent to the reranker
BM25 scores override reranker scores
The reranker only works with kNN child retrievers
blocks.explain: The reranker only sees the child retriever's top rank_window_size documents, 10 by default. Rank 15 sits outside the window, so this is the recall ceiling again, created by configuration. Set rank_window_size to the depth your budget allows.

lessons.title: The learned middle stage: a GBDT over many signals

blocks.md: A news search gets the query `election results`. Two articles match the words equally well, one from this morning and one from four years ago. A cross-encoder reads only the query and the text, so it cannot tell them apart; the publication date, the click history and the source's reputation never reach it. Production cascades therefore usually put a **learned feature-based stage** between retrieval and the neural reranker: a model that reads many numbers per candidate and combines them.

Each (query, document) pair becomes a **feature vector**: the first-stage scores and ranks (BM25, dense cosine, the RRF score), BM25 on each field separately (title, body), document length, freshness, popularity or past clicks, and any other cheap model score. *Feature engineering for ranking* covers how to build, normalize and log them. The model that combines them is most often **LambdaMART**: gradient-boosted decision trees (a GBDT, a sum of many small trees, each fitted to the errors of the ones before) trained with LambdaRank gradients, which weight each pair of documents with different labels by how much swapping the two would change nDCG. *Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART* derives it; here we care about where it sits in the cascade.

blocks.title: Where the GBDT sits

scenes.caption: Stage 1 fuses BM25 and dense lists. On SciFact the RRF of two top 100 lists holds 170.5 candidates on average.
Stage 2 looks up a feature vector for every candidate and scores it with a few hundred small trees: a handful of comparisons per tree, no transformer. It can afford all 170.
Only stage 2's top 30 go to the cross-encoder, which needs a full forward pass per pair. The GBDT decides who gets that expensive look.
Badges show time per query on this machine (CPU, 2 threads): the GBDT scores 170 candidates in about 0.2 ms; the cross-encoder needs about 250 ms for 30. That ratio is why the GBDT goes first.

blocks.md: We built this stage on SciFact. Each candidate in the RRF list (BM25 and all-MiniLM-L6-v2, top 100 each, k = 60, the setup of *Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval*) gets 8 features: its BM25, MiniLM and bge-small-en-v1.5 scores and ranks in each model's top 1000, its RRF score and its length in words. bge-small (from BAAI, the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence) is a third embedding model that was not used to retrieve; adding signals like that is exactly what this stage is for. XGBoost, a widely used open-source gradient-boosting library, implements LambdaMART as its `rank:ndcg` objective. Rows are grouped by query with `qid`, sorted, and the hyperparameters were fixed before looking at test.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np, xgboost as xgb

# one row per (query, candidate); rows sorted by query id
X_tr = np.vstack([r["X"] for r in train])        # 8 features per candidate
y_tr = np.concatenate([r["y"] for r in train])   # 1 if judged relevant
qid  = np.concatenate([[i] * len(r["y"]) for i, r in enumerate(train)])

ranker = xgb.XGBRanker(objective="rank:ndcg", tree_method="hist",
                       n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=4,
                       lambdarank_pair_method="topk",
                       lambdarank_num_pair_per_sample=10, n_jobs=2)
ranker.fit(X_tr, y_tr, qid=qid)                   # 809 train claims

def stage2(r):                                     # r: one test query
    s = ranker.predict(r["X"])
    return [r["cand"][i] for i in np.argsort(-s, kind="stable")]
blocks.caption: Condensed from the lab script. Training takes 1.6 s on this machine; the candidates are the RRF list of every train claim.

blocks.prompt: On the 300 test claims, RRF scores nDCG@10 0.718 and the cross-encoder replacing RRF's order on its top 20 drops it to 0.685 (from the hybrid search course). What will the GBDT stage score, and what happens if we then let the cross-encoder reorder the GBDT's top 30?
blocks.reveal:
In this run the GBDT lifts nDCG@10 to **0.741** (+0.024 over RRF, 59 claims up, 42 down, p = 0.035). Its recall@30 is 0.936 against RRF's 0.905, so the next stage also gets a better list.

Letting the cross-encoder **replace** that order on the top 30 falls to **0.686** (-0.055, p < 0.001): this MS MARCO model ranks scientific claims worse than the features do. The fix is in the next block.

blocks.md:
Instead of trusting the cross-encoder's order, make its score **one more feature**. A second GBDT, trained on the top 30 that stage 2 hands over, reads the 8 features plus the cross-encoder logit. In this run it scores **0.751**: +0.034 over RRF (p = 0.005), and +0.010 over stage 2 alone, which is not significant (p = 0.084; 95% bootstrap interval -0.001 to +0.022). On this dataset the reranker adds little, but as a feature it did no harm on average, unlike replacing the order (0.686).

Two details made this honest. The second GBDT was trained on lists produced by stage 2 models that had **not** seen those train claims (5-fold out-of-fold predictions), so it learned on the kind of list it will see at test time. And every choice was made on train; test was scored once.

blocks.title: SciFact test nDCG@10 through the learned cascade (this run)

scenes.caption: Stage 2 adds 0.024 over RRF (p = 0.035). XGBoost's gain importance (loss drop per split) is far highest for bge's rank (145), then BM25 rank (18) and RRF score (12): a hint that the extra bge signal does much of the work, untested by ablation.
The cross-encoder's own order on the top 30 loses 0.055. A stronger stage does not mean a later stage should overrule it.
Using the CE logit as a feature: 0.751, the best list in this run, though its edge over stage 2 alone is within noise.

blocks.md: This is how Wang, Lin and Metzler defined a cascade in the first place: each stage *adds* its contribution to the score, $f_T = \sum_t \alpha_t H_t$, rather than throwing away what earlier stages learned. Vespa supports the same pattern. Its docs show a rank profile whose first phase mixes text and a non-text signal and whose second phase is an XGBoost model:

blocks.caption: Adapted from Vespa's phased-ranking docs (their version also sets total-rerank-count: 50). The second phase reranks the 100 best first-phase hits per content node by default. The model's feature names must map to Vespa rank features, so the numbers it sees in serving are the ones it was trained on.

blocks.md: A global phase can then add a cross-encoder in ONNX and combine it with earlier values passed up as `match-features`, as in the docs' example `my_expensive_function + sum(onnx(my_ranking_model).out)`. Vespa's advice for choosing the phases is the cascade principle in one line: the full ranking function is usually too expensive for every match, so it belongs in the second phase, and the task is to find a first-phase function that correlates well enough with it.

The middle stage is where non-text signals and extra model scores enter, cheaply enough to score every candidate. Train each stage on the lists the previous stage really produces, and give later stages earlier scores as features instead of letting them overwrite the order.

Two traps. Training on features computed differently from serving (train/serve skew) silently breaks the model; log features at serving time and train on the logs. And labels from clicks are biased toward what was already ranked high: *Click models and unbiased learning to rank* shows how to correct that.

blocks.question: Why put the GBDT before the cross-encoder rather than after it?
options: Trees cannot read cross-encoder scores
LambdaMART requires BM25 to be the last feature computed
Cross-encoders need a GBDT score as input
The GBDT costs well under a millisecond for all candidates, so it can filter the long list and decide which few get the expensive model; after the cross-encoder it would only see the short list
blocks.explain: Cascades order stages by cost per document. On this machine the GBDT scored 170 candidates in about 0.2 ms while the cross-encoder needed about 250 ms for 30. A GBDT can also run after the cross-encoder, as our combiner did, but its first job is choosing who reaches the expensive stage.

blocks.question: In our run the cross-encoder's own order on stage 2's top 30 scored 0.686, but the same scores used as a GBDT feature gave 0.751. What explains the difference?
options: Using the logit as a feature lets the model weigh it against the first-stage signals learned from labels; replacing the order throws those signals away
The GBDT re-ran the cross-encoder at a longer max_length
The combined model saw the test labels
Cross-encoder logits must be sorted ascending
blocks.explain: The cross-encoder is a weaker judge of scientific claims than the fused signals, but not useless. As one feature among nine, trained on the train claims, it gets only as much weight as it earns. Nothing touched the test labels; the GBDT was trained on train claims only.

lessons.title: LLM listwise reranking as the final stage

blocks.md: monoBERT scores one document at a time (**pointwise**) and duoBERT compares two (**pairwise**). A **listwise** reranker looks at several candidates at once and outputs their order. RankGPT (Sun et al., EMNLP 2023, the Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing conference) does this with an instruction-following LLM: passages are given identifiers `[1]`, `[2]`, ... and the model is asked to output a permutation such as `[2] > [3] > [1]`, with no scores at all.

An LLM cannot read 100 passages in one prompt comfortably, so RankGPT uses a **sliding window** with window size $w$ and step $s$, moving from the **back** of the list to the front. For a list of $M$ candidates, it first reorders the last $w$ positions, $M-w+1$ to $M$, then slides up by $s$ and reorders again, until it reaches the top. The paper's experiments rerank BM25's top 100 with $w = 20$, $s = 10$.

blocks.title: One back-to-front pass: 8 passages, w = 4, s = 2

scenes.caption: Stage 1 order. Grades (0 to 3) are hidden from the model; we show them to follow the pass. The best passage, h (grade 3), sits last. Simplified: the LLM is assumed to sort each window perfectly.
Window 1 covers positions 5 to 8. The LLM sorts it: h jumps from 8 to 5.
Window 2 covers positions 3 to 6 (slid up by s = 2). h is carried along because windows overlap by w - s = 2, and climbs to 3.

Window 3 covers positions 1 to 4. h reaches the top and c (grade 2) is second: the top w - s = 2 are exactly right. But b (grade 0) at 4 still sits above e (grade 1): lower positions are only partly sorted.

blocks.caption: The first window covers the last w positions; each further window moves up s, so the other M - w positions need (M - w) divided by s more windows, rounded up. With M = 100, w = 20, s = 10: 8 + 1 = 9 LLM calls, reading 9 x 20 = 180 passages, nearly twice the list.

blocks.prompt: Assume the LLM sorts every window perfectly. After one back-to-front pass with w = 20 and s = 10, which part of the final list is guaranteed to be in the correct order?
blocks.reveal: Exactly the **top w - s = 10**. Each window hands its best w - s documents to the next window, so any document that belongs in the global top 10 is never left behind. Our simulation over 20,000 random lists with varied w and s found no exception. Below position 10 there is no guarantee, as b above e showed. That matches what you want from a final stage: a correct top, cheap tail.

blocks.md: The paper's ablations show the cascade logic inside the LLM stage. Results were highly sensitive to the initial order: starting from a random or reversed BM25 list hurt, because one pass relies on a decent starting order. Extra passes could raise nDCG@10 but lowered nDCG@1. On BEIR (a zero-shot benchmark of 18 retrieval datasets from different domains), letting GPT-4 rerank only the top 30 of ChatGPT's output gave good results at about a fifth of the cost of GPT-4 alone. The authors also flag cost, latency and unstable generation as obstacles to deploying LLM rerankers directly.

RankGPT is one of four prompting families. **Pointwise** prompts score each passage alone (one call per candidate, all in parallel), **pairwise** prompts compare two passages, **setwise** prompts pick the best of a few, and **listwise** prompts like RankGPT's order a window. They differ by orders of magnitude in calls, tokens and sequential rounds. *LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting* teaches each family, and *Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking* does the cost accounting. Open listwise models such as RankVicuna and RankZephyr, distilled from GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 orderings, run the same sliding window without an API. For the cascade, one rule carries over: put the LLM where the list is shortest.

A practical modern cascade: hybrid first stage (BM25 plus a distilled bi-encoder) with k in the hundreds, a small distilled cross-encoder on that list, and optionally an LLM listwise reranker on only the top 20 or 30. Log candidates and scores per stage so you can measure each stage's recall and gain separately.

blocks.question: RankGPT reranks M = 100 passages with w = 20 and s = 10. You switch to w = 20, s = 5 to give passages more chances to move. How many LLM calls does one pass now make?
blocks.explain: ceil((100 - 20) / 5) + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17 calls, reading 17 x 20 = 340 passages. Smaller steps mean more overlap and almost double the cost of s = 10. The guaranteed-correct top also grows, from w - s = 10 to 15.

blocks.question: Your LLM listwise reranker on the top 100 meets quality targets but costs too much per query. Which change follows the cascade principle best?
options: Run the LLM on the top 100 but with a random initial order to avoid bias
Drop stage 1 and let the LLM read the whole corpus in windows
Let a distilled cross-encoder rerank the 100 and send only its top 20 to the LLM in one window
Increase the step size to 20 so windows no longer overlap
blocks.explain: Put the cheap model where the list is long and the expensive model where it is short: one LLM window instead of 9 calls. RankGPT's own GPT-4-on-top-30 result follows the same pattern. Random initial order hurt in the paper, and s = w removes the overlap that carries good passages forward.

lessons.title: Distillation: moving a late stage's quality into an earlier one

blocks.md: The cascade puts a cheap model first and an expensive one last, and the quality gap between them is what the late stages fix. **Distillation** narrows that gap from the other side: the expensive model labels training data, and a cheaper model learns to copy its judgments, so the early stage hands better candidates to everything after it. Lesson 6's tip already used it (a distilled cross-encoder in the middle). This lesson works through the losses on numbers, then runs one distillation on SciFact.

**Distillation** turns an expensive stage into a teacher for a cheaper one. Run the slow model offline on training queries, then train a fast model to imitate its rankings. You pay the teacher's cost once, at training time, instead of on every query.

Three distillation recipes, each moving quality one stage earlier:

- **RankGPT permutation distillation**: ChatGPT ranks 20 BM25 candidates for 10,000 MS MARCO queries; a cross-encoder student is trained with RankNet, a pairwise ranking loss shown below, on the 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 ordered pairs per query. A roughly 440M-parameter DeBERTa (Microsoft's BERT variant, Decoding-enhanced BERT with disentangled attention) student beat the 3B monoT5 by 1.67 nDCG on average on BEIR.
- **Margin-MSE** (margin mean squared error; Hofstätter et al., 2020): cross-encoder teachers (BERT-CAT, for concatenated query and passage) train ColBERT, a BERT dot-product bi-encoder and others to match the teacher's score *margin* between a relevant and a non-relevant passage.
- **ColBERTv2**: a 22M-parameter MiniLM cross-encoder scores retrieved passages, and ColBERT is trained with a KL-divergence loss (explained next) toward those scores over 64 passages per example.

**KL (Kullback-Leibler) divergence** measures how far one probability distribution is from another. In ColBERTv2, the teacher's and the student's scores over the 64 passages are each turned into probabilities with a softmax, p from the teacher and q from the student. The loss is the sum over passages of p times log(p / q): 0 when the two match, positive otherwise. So the student learns the teacher's relative preferences among the passages, not its raw score values.

blocks.caption: Margin-MSE. Q is the query, P+ a relevant and P- a non-relevant passage; M_s is the student, M_t the teacher. Matching margins instead of raw scores lets each architecture keep its own score range; Hofstätter et al. saw very different ranges across architectures.
RankNet loss used for RankGPT's permutation distillation: r_i is the teacher's rank of passage i and s_i the student's score. Every pair the teacher ordered becomes a training signal.

blocks.md: Where the RankNet loss comes from: RankNet (Burges et al., 2005) models the probability that passage $i$ belongs above passage $j$ as the sigmoid of the score gap: 1 divided by 1 plus e raised to minus the gap $s_i - s_j$. Training uses cross-entropy with target 1 for every pair the teacher ordered, and minus the log of that sigmoid is exactly the log of 1 plus e raised to $s_j - s_i$, the formula above. It is near 0 when the student scores $i$ well above $j$ and grows almost linearly with the gap when the student has the pair backwards.

A toy with real arithmetic. One query, four passages, P1 relevant. The teacher cross-encoder's logits are 8, 5, 1 and -2, so it orders P1 > P2 > P3 > P4. A bi-encoder student gives dot products 30, 31, 27 and 26: it has P1 and P2 the wrong way round, and its scores live on a different scale. What does each of the three losses complain about?

blocks.title: Which pair each loss pushes hardest (toy)

scenes.caption: RankNet, log(1 + e^(s_j - s_i)) over the 6 pairs the teacher ordered. The misordered pair P1 vs P2 costs 1.31; correctly ordered pairs with a gap of 3 to 5 cost 0.05 or less. Total 1.72.

Margin-MSE on the three (P1, negative) pairs. P1 vs P2: teacher margin +3, student -1, loss 16. P1 vs P4 costs even more (36): the student orders it right, but its margin 4 is far from the teacher's 10.

blocks.md: Where the KL numbers come from: the softmax turns the teacher's logits into p = 0.952, 0.047, 0.001 and 0.000, and the student's dot products into q = 0.264, 0.718, 0.013 and 0.005. KL(p, q) = 1.09, almost all from P1's term, 0.952 x ln(0.952 / 0.264) = 1.22. The gradient of this loss with respect to each student score is q minus p, so the student is told to raise P1 and lower P2, and P3 and P4 barely matter.

blocks.title: How hard KL pushes each student score (toy)

scenes.caption: Teacher probabilities p after the softmax: 0.952, 0.047, 0.001, 0.000. Almost all of the mass is on P1.
Size of the KL gradient q - p on each student score: raise P1 by 0.688 (good), lower P2 by 0.671 (bad means pushed down). P3 and P4 get 0.012 and 0.005: the tail barely matters.

blocks.md: The three losses teach different things. RankNet only cares about order, so it spends its effort on misordered pairs. Margin-MSE also cares about the size of each gap, so it keeps pushing on pairs that are already in order. KL with a softmax cares about the top of the teacher's list and almost ignores the tail.

blocks.prompt: We distil the MS MARCO cross-encoder into all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on SciFact train with Margin-MSE and use the student as a first stage on the test claims. The teacher reorders MiniLM's top 100 to nDCG@10 0.682, above MiniLM's 0.645. Does the student improve, and which metric matters?
blocks.reveal: In this run it got **worse**. nDCG@10 fell from 0.645 to 0.582 (37 claims up, 79 down, p < 0.001) and recall@100, the number a first stage exists for, from 0.925 to 0.901 (not significant, p = 0.11). Watch recall@k of the student's list, not only nDCG@10: the student's job is to hand the next stage a complete list. The next block separates one cause with a control run and suggests another.

blocks.code:
from datasets import Dataset
from sentence_transformers import (SentenceTransformer, SentenceTransformerTrainer,
                                   SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments, losses)

# label = teacher(q, pos) - teacher(q, neg): cross-encoder logits, scored once offline
ds = Dataset.from_dict({"query": qs, "pos": pos, "neg": neg, "label": margins})

base = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", device="cpu")
student = SentenceTransformer(modules=[base[0], base[1]])  # drop Normalize: raw dot
args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(output_dir="distil", num_train_epochs=1,
        per_device_train_batch_size=16, learning_rate=2e-5, warmup_ratio=0.1,
        use_cpu=True, save_strategy="no", report_to=[])
SentenceTransformerTrainer(model=student, args=args, train_dataset=ds,
                           loss=losses.MarginMSELoss(student)).train()
blocks.caption: 2,757 (claim, relevant abstract, hard negative) triples from SciFact train: the teacher's 3 top-scored non-relevant abstracts per claim. An epoch took 220 to 293 s here (two runs). We dropped the model's normalization layer so dot products can reach the teacher's margins (a cosine gap is at most 2).

blocks.md:
A control run separates one cause. Dropping the normalization alone, before any training, already cost the student: 0.607 nDCG@10 instead of 0.645, most likely because the model was trained for cosines. Training then lost more (0.582). We did not isolate why. A likely contributor: on the train triples whose positive was among the 30 candidates the teacher scored, it preferred the hard negative in 869 of 2607 (33%), and Margin-MSE copies the teacher's margins, so it teaches those preferences too. No run tested this, and some of those negatives may be unlabelled positives.

The published recipes used teachers trained on the student's domain: MS MARCO cross-encoders teaching MS MARCO students. Before distilling, check the teacher against labels on your own data, exactly as the lab in lesson 8 checks every stage. A teacher that beats the student only modestly (0.682 against 0.645 here) and prefers a non-relevant abstract in a third of its training pairs is a risky source of signal.

blocks.question: Why does Margin-MSE train the student on score margins instead of making it reproduce the teacher's raw scores?
options: Different architectures settle on different score levels; matching the margin frees the student's absolute level while copying how far apart the teacher puts each pair
Raw scores are not available from cross-encoders
Margins are cheaper to compute at query time
MSE cannot be applied to raw scores
blocks.explain: A dot-product bi-encoder or ColBERT produces scores on a very different scale from a cross-encoder. Forcing the same raw values fights the architecture. Ranking only needs the student to separate relevant from non-relevant by the same amount, which is what the margin captures.

blocks.question: In the toy, the student already orders P1 above P4 (30 versus 26), yet Margin-MSE gives that pair its largest loss, 36. Why?
options: Margin-MSE ignores order and only looks at raw scores
P4 is the relevant passage, so the student has it backwards
It matches the size of the gap: the teacher's margin is 10 and the student's only 4, so the pair is ordered but not separated enough
The softmax inside Margin-MSE amplifies the bottom of the list
blocks.explain: Margin-MSE is (student margin - teacher margin) squared: (4 - 10) squared = 36. It reproduces the teacher's gaps, not just its order. RankNet gives the same pair only 0.018 because it is already ordered. There is no softmax in Margin-MSE; that is the KL loss.

lessons.title: Lab: measure a cascade stage by stage on SciFact

blocks.md:
Time to measure a cascade instead of reasoning about one. The setup is the one from *Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval*: BEIR's SciFact (5,183 abstracts; 809 train claims used only for choices, 300 test claims used only for reporting), BM25 and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as first stages, RRF with k = 60, and `cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2` at max_length 256 as the reranker. We reuse those runs, so the shared numbers match: BM25 0.677, MiniLM 0.645, RRF 0.718 nDCG@10.

The questions are the cascade's: how deep must stage 1 go, how deep should the reranker look, and where does the time go? Every number below came from one run on this machine, a CPU with two threads.

**Step 1: recall@k of each candidate list on its own** (lesson 2's ceiling). We take each retriever's top 1000 and, for the fused curve, RRF over both top 1000 lists, and compute recall@k at several depths.

blocks.title: SciFact test recall@k of each first stage (this run)

scenes.caption: k = 10: BM25 0.808, MiniLM 0.783, RRF 0.854. Fusion is ahead at every depth below 1000 because the two lists miss different abstracts.
k = 20: BM25 0.870, MiniLM 0.837, RRF 0.893. Recall still climbs quickly here.
k = 50: BM25 0.894, MiniLM 0.892, RRF 0.937. Recall still climbs quickly here.
k = 100: BM25 0.919, MiniLM 0.925, RRF 0.955. Each further step adds little: the curve is flattening.
k = 200: BM25 0.937, MiniLM 0.960, RRF 0.977. Each further step adds little: the curve is flattening.
k = 1000: BM25 0.977, MiniLM 0.993, RRF 0.993. At 1000 the dense list and the fusion meet, and BM25 still misses 2.3% of relevant abstracts.

blocks.md: Read the curve as a price list. Going from 50 to 100 fused candidates buys 1.8 points of recall for 50 more reranker inputs; 100 to 200 buys 2.2 for 100 more. Each extra candidate buys less, while each doubling doubles the reranker cost. BM25 alone needs between 200 and 500 candidates to reach what the fusion has at 100. That is the case for a hybrid stage 1 in one number.

**Step 2: sweep the rerank depth.** Cross-encoder scores are pointwise, so score every candidate once and any depth is just a re-sort. We also compute the *oracle*: a perfect reranker at the same depth, which moves every relevant candidate to the top. The oracle is the ceiling; the real model shows how much of it you get.

blocks.code:
def rerank_at(ranked, scores, k):          # scores: CE logit per candidate
    head = sorted(ranked[:k], key=lambda d: -scores[d])
    return head + ranked[k:]

def oracle_at(ranked, rel, k):            # perfect reranker, same depth
    head = sorted(ranked[:k], key=lambda d: -(d in rel))
    return head + ranked[k:]

for k in (5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200):
    real = [ndcg10(rerank_at(R[q], CE[q], k), rel[q]) for q in test]
    best = [ndcg10(oracle_at(R[q], rel[q], k), rel[q]) for q in test]
    print(k, round(np.mean(real), 4), round(np.mean(best), 4))
blocks.caption: R[q] is the RRF list (170.5 candidates on average), CE[q] the cached cross-encoder logits. Depth 200 means the whole list.

blocks.prompt: The oracle's nDCG@10 rises with depth, from 0.818 at k = 5 to 0.962 for the whole list. Will the real cross-encoder also improve as it sees more candidates?
blocks.reveal: No: it gets **worse** with depth. 0.708 at 5, 0.701 at 10, 0.685 at 20, 0.677 at 100 and 0.675 for the whole list, all below RRF's own 0.718. Every extra candidate is another chance for this MS MARCO model to promote a wrong abstract above a right one. Depth 10 beats depth 20 by 0.015 (43 claims up, 9 down, p = 0.005).

blocks.title: nDCG@10 by rerank depth on SciFact test (this run)

scenes.caption: Oracle: a perfect reranker at each depth. The ceiling rises with depth, exactly as lesson 2's recall argument says.
The real cross-encoder at the same depths falls from 0.708 to 0.675. The gap to the ceiling is the reranker's own error, and it grows with depth.

blocks.md: On MS MARCO, with monoBERT reranking BM25, deeper lists helped with diminishing returns (lesson 2). Here the reranker is the bottleneck, not recall: depth 100 is 0.008 below depth 20 (not significant, p = 0.174), and the whole list loses another 0.002 on 6 claims and gains on none. The right depth is a property of *this* reranker on *this* data, and only a sweep shows it. The previous lessons' fix applies: a learned middle stage reached 0.741, and the cross-encoder as a feature 0.751 (lesson 5). An LLM listwise reranker on the top 20 would be the next thing to try; it is not run here (no GPU or LLM API in this lab), see *LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting*.

**Step 3: time each stage.** Median per query over 60 test claims on this machine: BM25 0.3 ms (a sparse matrix over 5,183 abstracts, not a full search engine), dense retrieval 3.2 ms (encode the claim, then a dot product with every abstract vector), RRF 0.07 ms, and the cross-encoder 250 ms for 30 pairs or 804 ms for 100. The GBDT averages 0.2 ms for 170 candidates. Encoding the corpus took 42 s, once, offline.

blocks.title: Where one query's time goes (this machine, CPU)

scenes.caption: Retrieval, fusion and the GBDT together finish in about 3.4 ms (BM25 and dense run side by side). They are too thin to see at this scale.
Add the cross-encoder on 30 pairs: about 250 ms, nearly all of the query on this CPU.
Reranking 100 instead: 804 ms, and on SciFact for a worse list. At the model card's V100 rate of 1,800 docs/s, 30 pairs would take about 17 ms: still the largest stage.

blocks.md:
**Pitfall: holes in the judgments.** Test collections judge only documents that some system once retrieved; everything else counts as non-relevant. A new stage that surfaces different documents is then punished for **holes**, unjudged documents in its top 10. BEIR measured this on TREC-COVID: BM25 had 6.4% unjudged documents in its top 10 (Hole@10), the dense retriever TAS-B 31.8%. After the authors judged the holes, TAS-B's nDCG@10 rose from 0.481 to 0.555, BM25's only from 0.656 to 0.668.

SciFact's qrels list only relevant abstracts (339 for the 300 test claims), so you cannot even count holes: judged and unjudged non-relevant look the same. Inspect a sample of a new stage's top results by hand before trusting a drop.

blocks.code:
import json, time

def search_logged(qid, query, log):
    rec = {"qid": qid, "t": time.time(), "stages": []}
    for name, stage, keep in [("rrf", stage1, 170), ("gbdt", stage2, 30),
                              ("final", stage3, 10)]:
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        cands, scores = stage(query, prev=rec)   # each stage sees the last
        rec["stages"].append({"name": name, "ms": 1000 * (time.perf_counter() - t0),
                              "ids": cands[:keep], "scores": scores[:keep]})
    log.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")
    return rec["stages"][-1]["ids"]
blocks.caption: A sketch of per-stage logging (stage1 to stage3 stand for your own functions). With every stage's candidates, scores and time on disk you can compute recall@k of each stage on labeled queries, replay a new reranker offline, and see which stage a latency spike came from.

blocks.md: Measure a cascade the way it runs: recall@k of each candidate list, quality after each stage on the same queries with paired tests, a depth sweep against the oracle ceiling, and time per stage. In our SciFact run the sweep showed the reranker, not recall, was the bottleneck, which no amount of reasoning from MS MARCO would have predicted.

blocks.question: You swap in a stronger dense first stage. Recall@100 rises from 0.90 to 0.95, yet nDCG@10 after reranking drops. What should you check first?
options: Whether the reranker's max_length is too short
Whether recall@100 was computed with the wrong k
Whether the GPU is slower than before
Whether the new top 10 contains many unjudged documents (holes) that the old pool never saw, which count as non-relevant
blocks.explain: A first stage that finds different documents is exactly when holes appear: BEIR's TAS-B had 31.8% unjudged documents in its top 10 on TREC-COVID, and judging them raised its nDCG@10 by 0.074. Check Hole@10 (or judge a sample) before concluding the system got worse. If holes are rare, then look at the reranker.

blocks.question: Our depth sweep scored 0.701 at depth 10, 0.685 at 20 and 0.677 at 100, while the oracle rose from 0.854 to 0.949. What does this tell you?
options: The reranker's ordering errors, not missing candidates, limit quality here; deeper lists give it more chances to promote wrong documents
Stage 1 recall is the bottleneck, so raise k
The oracle numbers must be wrong because they exceed 0.9
nDCG@10 cannot be compared across depths
blocks.explain: The oracle shows that the relevant abstracts are in the list, and more of them as depth grows. The real model gets worse anyway (10 against 20 is significant, p = 0.005; 20 against 100 is not, p = 0.174), so its judgments are the problem. Better options: a reranker suited to the domain, a combiner that keeps first-stage signals (lesson 5), or a shallow depth.
